entries.storyTitle: Home Assistant is an open-source home automation platform running on Python 3
entries.outcome: Grew to 2 million households and became the leading open-source home automation platform.
entries.outcomeDetail: Home Assistant's integration count exploded, and Nabu Casa built a sustainable business around it. In 2025 the project reported 2 million households, double its prior year.
entries.note: The joke was about light switches. Home Assistant's bet was that the value is stitching dozens of incompatible devices into one local control plane—which is exactly what happened.
entries.sourceLabel: Home Assistant / State of the Open Home 2025

entries.storyTitle: Show HN: Obsidian – A knowledge base that works on local Markdown files
entries.outcome: Reached roughly 1 million users while remaining 100% user-supported, with no VC funding.
entries.outcomeDetail: Obsidian stayed closed source but won users with local Markdown files, a huge plugin ecosystem, and optional sync and publish services. By 2023 it estimated about one million users, and its CEO says the company is entirely user-supported.
entries.note: The openness worry was legitimate, and Obsidian is still proprietary. But 'useless' badly underestimated how much users would trade for local files and a fast, extensible editor.

entries.storyTitle: Caddy – HTTP/2 Web Server with Automatic HTTPS
entries.outcome: Became a widely used web server with 79k+ GitHub stars and automatic HTTPS as its signature feature.
entries.outcomeDetail: Caddy 2 shipped in 2020 with a cleaner architecture and is now a common default in self-hosted and container stacks. W3Techs counted Caddy on 0.2% of scanned sites by 2026—hundreds of thousands of sites—and the project passed 79,000 GitHub stars.
entries.note: The 'patchwork' critique missed that Caddy's composition was the point: automatic TLS and a tiny config beat reimplementing Apache. Nginx later added more automation, but Caddy kept its niche.

entries.author: leftnode
entries.cardQuote: I feel pitching this as an open source alternative to Calendly is the wrong angle. The only people who care about open source are developers who are the least likely people to need scheduling software.
entries.quote:
Congratulations on launching. My (small) startup is a Calendly user for our sales and support staff. What would cause me to switch from Calendly to your product?

I would never want to self host this. We're a small team, and no one technical wants to manage yet another server, nor do we want the responsibility for when something screws up and a salesperson misses a demo or a support staff member isn't reminded about a training session.

The pricing isn't that competitive with Calendly ($3/user/month savings) which would translate to a savings of $108 annually for us, not enough to justify switching.

I feel pitching this as an open source alternative to Calendly is the wrong angle. The only people who care about open source are developers who are the least likely people to need scheduling software. And people who do need Calendly aren't going to be moved to switch because Calendly works well enough already.

Finally, the copy at the bottom of the page reads:

> For instance, booking a COVID vaccine shouldn't happen on a server in another country that somebody else is in control of.

Are people using Calendly to book COVID vaccines? If I used your product instead, wouldn't I still be booking a vaccine on someone else's server?

I wish any small competitor success against a large incumbent, but I would radically change my approach to compete against Calendly.
entries.storyTitle: Calendso: An open source Calendly alternative
entries.outcome: Raised a $25M Series A in 2022 and became the leading open-source scheduling platform.
entries.outcomeDetail: Cal.com (formerly Calendso) raised $25M led by Seven Seven Six at a reported $150M post-money valuation. In 2026 it announced it would close its core codebase, a separate controversy.
entries.note: The pricing and self-hosting points were fair. The claim that developers are the least likely people to need scheduling software was not: developer-facing scheduling and API-first booking became Cal.com's wedge.

entries.author: tannhaeuser
entries.cardQuote: A "headless" CMS is just an API server eg. a tool for JS developers; you could use any JSON or GraphQL API wrapping tool you want (PostgREST, say), or code one yourself in a few lines of code.
entries.quote: Is that meant as satire or what? Structured content that an end-user can edit, query, share, comprehend, design, etc. is what you have with markup languages, and have had since over 30 years (SGML/HTML/XML). A "headless" CMS is just an API server eg. a tool for JS developers; you could use any JSON or GraphQL API wrapping tool you want (PostgREST, say), or code one yourself in a few lines of code. So I have to say "headless CMS" is really a pure marketing term, and IMHO utter pointless, as the difficulty and most of the work in a CMS product comes from a front-end (or architectural match, really) that end users can meaningfully interact with and set up dynamic sites, redactional workflows, dynamic user content, theming, analytics+banners, asset management/pipelines, etc., etc. with.
entries.outcome: Raised a $31M Series B in 2022 and became one of the most widely used open-source headless CMSes.
entries.outcomeDetail: Strapi's admin UI, content modeling, and REST/GraphQL APIs found a large audience. The company raised $31M led by CRV, bringing total funding to about $45M, and the project passed 70,000 GitHub stars.
entries.note: The 'just an API server' reduction ignored the hard parts Strapi actually shipped: an editor-friendly admin, permissions, media handling, and a plugin system. Those are the parts teams did not want to rebuild.

entries.storyTitle: Show HN: Appwrite – Open-Source and Self Hosted Firebase Alternative
entries.outcome: Raised a $27M Series A in 2022 and grew past 150,000 developers.
entries.outcomeDetail: Appwrite's one-command self-hosting and Firebase-like auth, database, storage, and functions found a large audience. The company raised $27M led by Tiger Global and later launched Appwrite Cloud; the repo has 58,000+ stars.

entries.quote: Only one filter.  Very fast limited search.  Not great for anything remotely complex like searching with two conditions.
entries.storyTitle: MeiliSearch: Zero-config alternative to Elasticsearch, made in Rust
entries.outcome: Raised a $15M Series A in 2022 and became a leading lightweight search engine with 59k+ GitHub stars.
entries.outcomeDetail: Meilisearch added multi-filter support, faceting, and hybrid search, while keeping its fast, low-config setup. It raised $15M led by Felicis and is widely used for site and app search.
entries.note: The single-filter limit was real at launch and Meilisearch fixed it. The broader dismissal missed that 'limited but fast' was exactly the trade-off a large group of app developers wanted.

entries.author: jillesvangurp
entries.cardQuote: When it comes to ranking quality, a one size fits all, non sharded solution like this is definitely not going to stand up to much scrutiny.
entries.quote:
What do you mean not fast enough? Lucene/Elasticsearch/Solr are basically routinely used on datasets that are way beyond the scope of what this or Algolia is used on (i.e. petabyte scale). I've worked with teams indexing billions of documents. At that scale measuring ranking quality is a much bigger concern than raw performance, which is just a matter of throwing more hardware at it (i.e. it's more of a cost concern than a performance concern). When it comes to ranking quality, a one size fits all, non sharded solution like this is definitely not going to stand up to much scrutiny. Either it fits, or more likely it doesn't and you need the knobs to tune it (which Lucene provides you plenty of).

Most of the tricks that Algolia and (presumably) this product do to be fast have more to do with how they manage memory than with their implementation language. Basically, Algolia is a non sharded search index that is loaded into memory in its entirety. They don't have to worry about disk seeks, file cache misses, etc. Not a problem when your entire index fits in memory. Of course that puts an upper limit on what they can index and limits the uses to smallish datasets that in no way pose any challenge whatsoever to Lucene (especially when your index easily fits in memory).

I'm not saying it's a bad approach. I think it's a great approach for smallish data sets with very loose ranking requirements where a one size fits all solution does the job and is good enough. For many companies search is not really core to their experience and it just needs to be idiot proof and low hassle to set up for their non expert tech teams and product managers.
entries.outcome: Typesense Cloud now serves more than 10 billion searches a month; the project has 27k+ GitHub stars.
entries.outcomeDetail: Typesense stayed bootstrapped and focused on fast, typo-tolerant search for small and mid-sized datasets. Its hosted service crossed 10 billion searches per month, and the open-source engine remains a common Algolia alternative.
entries.note: The scale analysis was technically sound—Typesense is not built for petabyte datasets. But most search workloads are exactly the 'smallish' kind he dismissed, and Typesense won plenty of them.

entries.storyTitle: Show HN: Plausible – Self-Hosted Google Analytics alternative
entries.outcome: Reached $1M ARR in 2022 and became one of the leading privacy-first analytics tools.
entries.outcomeDetail: Plausible stayed bootstrapped and profitable, passed $1M ARR in June 2022, and says it has never raised investor money. Its daily-rotating hash design remains a deliberate accuracy trade-off.
entries.note: The limitation was real: Plausible cannot follow a user across days, so long conversion windows are fuzzy. But most sites wanted simple, privacy-friendly traffic numbers, and that market was much larger than the critic assumed.

entries.storyTitle: Windmill: Open-source developer platform to turn scripts into workflows and UIs
entries.outcome: Grew to 10,663 instances and 300+ enterprise customers, including Zoom and Kahoot.
entries.outcomeDetail: Windmill kept its Deno-based runtime but added Python, Go, Bash, SQL, and more, plus Git sync and enterprise controls. Its site reports 10,663 instances and 300+ enterprise customers, with case studies from Zoom, Photoroom, and Investing.com.
entries.note: The risk warning was reasonable for 2023. Windmill reduced it by supporting many languages and by landing large reference customers instead of asking teams to bet only on Deno.

entries.storyTitle: Gitea – A community-managed fork of Gogs
entries.outcome: Grew to 59k+ GitHub stars; its Forgejo fork was adopted by Codeberg and FFmpeg.
entries.outcomeDetail: Gitea became the default lightweight self-hosted Git forge and later spawned Forgejo, which Codeberg uses and FFmpeg moved to in 2025. Gogs, by contrast, stagnated.
entries.note: The fork was not a quality regression; it was a governance fix for a single-maintainer bottleneck. Gitea's codebase and community both outgrew the original.

entries.quote: Metabase is nowhere close to being a business-ready BI tool. I wish them luck, but their current product is basically a tech demo compared to the real, commercial products out there -- none of which require you to put your data anywhere in particular either (you can run Tableau against pretty much any DB platform out there).
entries.storyTitle: Show HN: Metabase, an open-source business intelligence tool
entries.outcome: Raised a $30M Series B in 2021 and became a leading open-source BI platform with 50k+ GitHub stars.
entries.outcomeDetail: Metabase kept its simple question-and-dashboard workflow, added models, permissions, and embedding, and grew into a standard self-hosted BI tool. Insight Partners led a $30M Series B in 2021.
entries.note: At launch it was rough, and the 'tech demo' label was not crazy. But Metabase optimized for non-analysts who wanted answers without a warehouse project—and that was a huge, underserved market.

Reproducing functionality and growing an idea is fine. It's the blatant disregard to UX and UI where this company has literally pixel for pixel ripped off slack.
entries.outcome: Raised a $50M Series B in 2019 and became a major self-hosted Slack alternative for security-conscious enterprises.
entries.outcomeDetail: Mattermost leaned into self-hosting, security, and compliance, winning customers that could not use Slack. Y Combinator Continuity led a $50M Series B in 2019, and the project remains a standard option for air-gapped team chat.
entries.note: The UI was derivative, and that was the critic's whole point. But the buying criteria in regulated environments were deployment control and auditability, not original pixels.

entries.quote: ZeroTier is also open-source. If TailScale isn't then I personally wouldn't even consider it a competitor.
entries.storyTitle: TailScale – Instantly interconnect your devices and services, wherever they are
entries.outcome: Raised a $160M Series C in 2025 and became a leading corporate VPN replacement.
entries.outcomeDetail: Tailscale open-sourced its client and built a huge business on its coordination service, with a free personal tier and enterprise SSO and ACL features. The Series C was led by Accel, and Tailscale reported rapid growth in corporate VPN replacement.
entries.note: The open-source purity test was a poor predictor of adoption. Tailscale's clients are open, the hard part is the control plane, and 'just use WireGuard' turned out to be much harder than it looks.

entries.author: educar
entries.cardQuote: I feel sad for ownCloud and Nextcloud. ownCloud has a brand and this fork dilutes it. It will be on everyone's mind especially since the founder has left to create a competitor.
entries.quote: I feel sad for ownCloud and Nextcloud. ownCloud has a brand and this fork dilutes it. It will be on everyone's mind especially since the founder has left to create a competitor. For Nextcloud, unless they can explicitly state why this fork exists, it's hard to side with them. What kind of ideological differences are we talking about? Sure, you don't need to throw around personal accusations or finger point but it would help to know what motivated this. On a related note, this is a risk which many platform companies take. If you opensource your project completely, then anyone can fork it and take it ahead if the forker is a big or well known person. I think we got really lucky with iojs and node.
entries.storyTitle: Owncloud has been forked into Nextcloud
entries.outcome: Became the most widely deployed open-source content collaboration platform, used by EU governments.
entries.outcomeDetail: Nextcloud took most of ownCloud's contributors and quickly won public-sector and enterprise deployments. The European Commission described it as the most widely deployed open-source content collaboration platform, and Germany, France, Sweden, and the Netherlands adopted it.
entries.note: The brand worry was backwards: ownCloud Inc. collapsed within hours of the fork, while Nextcloud became the brand that mattered. Forking was the rescue, not the dilution.

entries.author: kahnclusions
entries.cardQuote: Jellyfin is buggy and laggy and full of security issues... it's difficult to even play content on my TV. Music doesn't even play on Android app without some weird jittering bug. Plex just works.
entries.quote: I've tried Jellyfin but still using Plex. As much as I hate Plex with a passion, it does work. Jellyfin is buggy and laggy and full of security issues... it's difficult to even play content on my TV. Music doesn't even play on Android app without some weird jittering bug. Plex just works. It's interface kind of sucks, and it has its occasional hiccups, and they insult your Taiwanese content with "Taiwan, Province of China", but at the very least it does what it claims to do... play my content.
entries.outcome: Became the leading free software media server, with 59k+ GitHub stars and a large self-hosting community.
entries.outcomeDetail: Jellyfin's clients, transcoding, and plugin ecosystem improved steadily, and it became the default recommendation for people leaving Plex. It remains community-run, with no paid tiers or account requirement.
entries.note: The bugs were real, especially on some TV clients. But the critic's own complaint—Plex's politics and account requirements—is exactly what drove users to tolerate rough edges and help Jellyfin improve.
